Also matches: méthode traditionnelle; methode traditionnelle; Champagne method
Definition: The way Champagne is made: the second fermentation, which makes the bubbles, happens inside each bottle. It gives fine bubbles and bready, brioche notes from time on the lees.

Short for pétillant naturel: a sparkling wine bottled before its first fermentation finishes, so the bubbles come from that one fermentation. Usually lightly fizzy, often cloudy, fruity and low in alcohol.
Sparkling wine made by a second fermentation in a large sealed tank, as for most Prosecco. It keeps the wine fruity and fresh, without the bready notes of the traditional method.
"White from whites": a sparkling wine made only from white grapes, usually Chardonnay. Typically lean, citrusy and fine.
"White from blacks": a white sparkling wine made from black grapes (Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier) pressed gently so the juice stays pale. Fuller and red-fruited.
The small amount of sweetened wine added to a sparkling wine just before it is corked. It sets how dry the wine tastes: the lower the dosage, the drier.

Also matches: no added sugar; zero dosage; pas dosé; pas dose
Definition: A sparkling wine with no dosage (no sugar added before corking): the driest style there is.
The spent yeast left after fermentation. Leaving wine in contact with it adds texture and bready, nutty flavours.
A Champagne made by the family that farms the vines, rather than by a large house buying grapes. Usually from one village or a few plots, with more character from place and vintage.
Spain's traditional-method sparkling wine, mostly from Catalonia, usually from Macabeo, Parellada and Xarel·lo.
German for sparkling wine. The best, like this one, are made by the traditional method from Riesling.
French traditional-method sparkling wine made outside Champagne, for example in Alsace, the Loire or Burgundy.

Wine made with as little added or taken away as possible: farmed organically, fermented with the wild yeast on the grapes, and bottled with little or no added sulfur. Can taste wilder, cloudier or funkier than classic wine.
Made with as few additions and treatments as possible in the winery. Close in meaning to natural.
Grown without synthetic fertilisers, weedkillers or pesticides. In the EU an organic wine must be certified.
Organic farming plus a set of extra practices: herbal and mineral preparations, and timing work by the moon and seasons. The vineyard is run as one living system.

Also matches: no sulfur; sans soufre; zero sulfur; no added sulphur
Definition: Sulfur dioxide protects wine from oxygen and bacteria. Wines made without adding any taste fresher and more vibrant, but can be less stable, so keep them cool.
Made with only a small addition of sulfur dioxide, the usual preservative.
Leaving the juice of white grapes on their skins, as for red wine. It adds colour (gold to amber), grip and flavours of dried fruit, tea and peel. Long skin contact makes an orange wine.
A white wine made like a red: fermented on its grape skins. Amber in colour, with some tannin and grip. Also called skin-contact or amber wine.
A traditional Spanish style made by fermenting white and red grapes together. Sits between a rosé and a light red.
Different grape varieties grown mixed together in one vineyard and picked and fermented together.
Fermenting red grapes with their stems still on. It brings perfume, a spicy, herbal lift and fresher-feeling tannins.
Fermenting whole, uncrushed red grapes in a tank filled with carbon dioxide. It gives soft, juicy, very fruity wines, as in much Beaujolais.

Also matches: barrel fermented; barrel-fermentation; barrel ageing; barrel aging; barrel-aged; barrel aged
Definition: Fermented or aged in oak barrels rather than steel tanks. It adds texture and, from newer barrels, flavours of toast, vanilla and spice.
Wine aged in oak barrels. New oak gives vanilla, toast and spice; old oak mainly adds texture and gentle air contact.
Made and aged without oak, usually in steel or concrete, so the fruit tastes pure and fresh.
A clay pot for fermenting or ageing wine, an ancient method. Clay lets in a little air without adding flavour.
Concrete tanks or eggs for fermenting and ageing. Like oak they let the wine breathe slightly, but add no flavour.

Also matches: casks; large old casks; foudre; foudres
Definition: A large wooden barrel. Big, old casks add almost no oak flavour; they mainly let the wine age gently.
Jura wine whose barrels are kept full, so no air reaches it. It stays fresh, unlike the nutty, sherry-like wines aged under flor.
Deliberately exposed to some air during ageing, giving nutty, bruised-apple and sherry-like flavours and a deeper colour.
A layer of yeast that grows on wine in barrels that are not topped up, as in sherry and Jura's vin jaune. It gives salty, nutty, almond flavours.
Tasting of nuts, bruised apple and salt, like a dry sherry. Comes from flor or from oxidative ageing.
Wine with grape spirit added, which raises the alcohol and, if added during fermentation, keeps natural sweetness. Port and Maury are fortified.
Grapes left on the vine until well after the normal harvest so they shrivel and their sugar concentrates. Makes rich, sweet wines.
A German ripeness category: grapes picked late and selected bunch by bunch. Usually sweet, sometimes with noble rot.
A German ripeness category meaning "late harvest". Riper than standard, from off-dry to sweet.
German for dry.
A region of north-east Hungary and south-east Slovakia, famous for sweet wines from Furmint grapes affected by noble rot.
A mould that, in the right misty autumn weather, shrivels ripe grapes and concentrates their sugar and acidity. It gives honey, apricot and marmalade flavours to sweet wines.

Also matches: old vine; old-vine; vieilles vignes; vieille vigne; vinhas velhas
Definition: Vines decades old (there is no legal minimum age). They give fewer, smaller grapes, often with more concentration.
Vines in their first years, which give lighter, fresher wines. Producers often bottle them separately from their top wine.
Made from the grapes of one named vineyard, so it shows that site's particular character.
In Burgundy, wine named after its village (such as Ladoix or Volnay). A step above regional Bourgogne and below premier cru and grand cru.
"First growth": in Burgundy and Champagne, a vineyard or village officially rated just below grand cru.
The top official vineyard rating in Burgundy and Champagne.
A legally protected wine name tied to a place, with rules on grapes, yields and methods. Sancerre and Chablis are appellations.
The simplest French wine category, with no rules on region or grapes. Many natural winemakers use it to work outside appellation rules.
A particular blend or bottling from a producer, usually with its own name.
A winery owned jointly by many local growers who bring their grapes to make wine together.
A merchant who buys grapes or wine from growers and makes, bottles and sells it under their own name.

Also matches: volcanic soil; volcanic soils; volcanic ash
Definition: Vineyards on soils from old eruptions. Often linked with smoky, salty, mineral-tasting wines with firm acidity.
A soft white limestone, the famous soil of Champagne and Sancerre. Chalk-grown wines tend to be fine, fresh and lean.
A dark, flaky rock, as on the steep Mosel slopes. Slate-grown Riesling is often described as stony and smoky.
A hard, crumbly rock that drains well, as in the best Beaujolais villages. Granite-grown wines are often fresh and perfumed.
A rock rich in calcium, as in Burgundy. Associated with tense, mineral, long-lived wines.
A tasting word for flavours that are not fruit: wet stone, chalk, flint, salt. Usually goes with high acidity and a lean style.
A smoky, flinty smell from the winemaking (a little sulfur reduction), prized in some top Chardonnay and Champagne.
A smell like kerosene that develops in aged Riesling. Prized by Riesling lovers; some guests find it odd, so mention it.
Tasting like still wine: for a sparkling wine, rich and full-flavoured rather than light and fizzy.
The slight drying or rough feel on the gums and tongue from tannin. Gentle grip is pleasant; strong grip needs food.
Compounds from grape skins, seeds, stems and oak that dry the mouth, like strong tea. Mostly in red and orange wines. Scored 1 to 5 on the card.
The freshness or sharpness of a wine: it makes your mouth water. High-acid wines taste crisp and lively. Scored 1 to 5 on the card.
How heavy a wine feels in the mouth, from light like skimmed milk to full like cream. Alcohol, sugar and extract all add body. Scored 1 to 5 on the card.
How much sugar you can taste, from dry (none) to luscious. Off-dry means a hint of sweetness. Scored 1 to 5 on the card.
This tool's score for natural-wine character: from clean and classic (1) to divisive (5), with cloudiness, funk or volatility. Warn guests about anything at 4 or 5.
Flavours that are not fruit or sweet: herbs, meat, earth, mushroom, salt.
Light and high in acidity, with little fat or richness. Not a fault: think Chablis or Muscadet.
How a wine feels rather than tastes: smooth, waxy, creamy, grippy. Lees, skin contact and oak all add texture.
Having firm tannin and acidity that frame the fruit. Structured wines usually need food or time.
How long the flavour lasts after you swallow. Long length is a sign of quality.
